segments.text: In 2019, Facebook was fined five billion dollars. The largest penalty in FTC history. Eighty-seven million people's data — harvested, profiled, and sold to a political targeting firm without their knowledge. And on the day the fine was announced, Facebook's stock went up. The market added six billion dollars in value. Mark Zuckerberg personally gained one point one billion dollars in a single day. The punishment made the company richer than if the government had done nothing.
segments.notes: Cold open. Four beats match the four [beat] markers. Beat 1: news footage of the FTC announcement — entity-specific, no generic corporate imagery. Beat 2: stat card ('Here is what five billion dollars') makes the number concrete. Beat 3: data center for the 87M people — scale and abstraction. Beat 4: stock chart going UP is the thesis in one image — the reversal that demands explanation. Impact SFX fires on '$5 billion.' Pause after the stock-went-up line — let the audience sit with the wrongness of it.

segments.text: How is that possible?
segments.notes: Single rhetorical beat — do not over-cut. The [pause] marker is BEFORE this question: 1.5s dead air after 'stock went up,' then Zuckerberg's face at the Senate hearing as the question drops. His expression during testimony is pure irony — he's the answer to his own question. No SFX, no overlay. Silence is the editorial choice.

segments.text: To understand, you need to go back to 1977. Because someone had to discover this trick. And the discovery started with a car on fire.
segments.notes: Three beats for the one [beat] marker plus two natural sentence breaks. The time-jump needs immediate visual anchoring — Ford Pinto first. 'The trick' gets a math formula image: this is not metaphor, it IS a formula, tease that visually before the chapter reveals it. Crash test image on the cliffhanger 'started with a car' — cuts directly into the chapter card. Whoosh SFX fires on the year-jump. '1977' text overlay stamps the date. No pause after — let momentum carry into chapter transition.

segments.text: [CHAPTER: THE FORMULA]

beats.text: [CHAPTER: THE FORMULA]

segments.notes: LearnByLeo 5-step chapter transition: punch (end of seg 2) → 3s silence → card → new energy → hook. Fade to black going in. Formula image plays on V1 as texture behind the chapter card on V3. Music rises during the card — the only moment in this block where music is not ducked. After the card, music drops back under for seg 4 narration.

segments.text: In 1977, Ford knew the Pinto's fuel tank ruptured in rear-end collisions. They had the crash test data. Two engineers wrote a cost-benefit analysis — an actual document, with actual numbers. Fix every Pinto: one hundred and thirty-seven million dollars. Expected wrongful death payouts: forty-nine point five million. They shipped the car.

beats.text: In 1977, Ford knew the Pinto's fuel tank ruptured in rear-end collisions.
They had the crash test data.
Two engineers wrote a memo.

segments.notes: Three beats for the two [beat] markers. Entity-specific throughout — all Ford Pinto imagery. Beat 1: fuel tank crash test photo establishes the engineering reality. Beat 2: actual crash test documents for 'they had the data' — the paperwork condemns them before the formula does. Beat 3: recall notice for 'two engineers wrote a memo' — the closest available visual to an internal document. No SFX here — saving audio impact for the crash in seg 5. Pause after 'memo' creates anticipation for the cost-benefit formula reveal.

segments.text: A thirteen-year-old boy named Richard Grimshaw was a passenger in a Pinto that was rear-ended in San Bernardino. The fuel tank ruptured. The driver burned to death. Richard survived — barely. Burned over his entire body. Lost parts of his fingers. Lost his left ear. Years of skin grafts. A childhood replaced by hospital rooms. The jury awarded one hundred and twenty-five million dollars in punitive damages — the largest in American history. The judge reduced it to three point five million. Ford was acquitted of criminal homicide. No executive went to prison.

beats.text: A thirteen-year-old boy named Richard Grimshaw was a passenger in a Pinto.
It was rear-ended in San Bernardino.
The fuel tank exploded.
Richard survived. With burns over ninety percent of his body.

sfx.motivation: Impact on the collision — visceral and short. The physical reality of the crash landing on the audience.

segments.notes: Four beats match the four [beat] markers — this is the highest-tension sequence in the chapter. Beat 1: Grimshaw court case image anchors the name — 'face' zoom targets the human being, not the car. 'RICHARD GRIMSHAW' text overlay fires here — LearnByLeo character introduction rule. Beat 2: archival crash image for the rear-end. Beat 3: the 5-second explosion clip — only 5s of source, fits exactly one beat, let audio play for 3s then cut back under VO. Beat 4: survivor disfigurement image holds on 'burns over ninety percent' — do not cut away from this. Body impact SFX on the collision beat, fires before the explosion clip to anticipate it.

segments.text: The fine was three point five million dollars. Ford kept selling cars. No one went to prison. And somewhere in a boardroom, someone noticed something. The cost of getting caught was less than the cost of doing the right thing.

beats.text: The fine was three point five million dollars.
Ford kept selling cars.
No one went to prison.
And somewhere in a boardroom, someone did the math.

segments.notes: Four beats. After the emotional peak of Grimshaw's burns, this segment delivers the institutional cold. '$3.5 MILLION' text overlay fires on beat 1 — audience has already seen '$5 BILLION' (seg 0), the contrast builds the ratio argument before it's stated. Beat 2: Ford Pinto still (the car kept moving — terrible visual irony). Beat 3: courtroom gavel is the absence of justice made visible. Beat 4: boardroom image on 'someone did the math' — hold here, zoom in slow. Pause after is anticipation for the formula itself. No SFX — the silence after the crash SFX in seg 5 makes this institutional coldness feel worse.

segments.text: That might have been an isolated scandal. A single bad company making a single bad calculation. Except it wasn't.

beats.text: That might have been an isolated scandal.
A single bad company making a single bad calculation.
Except it wasn't.

segments.notes: Three beats. The [pause] marker is BEFORE this segment — 1.5s after the boardroom calculation line, then this pivot begins. Beat 1: generic fines/money stack image — deliberately ordinary, 'maybe it was just one company.' Beat 2: financial fines profit chart — still ambiguous, still building the premise. Beat 3: the trillion-dollar aggregate image on 'Except it wasn't' — scale reveal, the thesis lands visually. Shimmer SFX fires on 'Except it wasn't' — shimmer rather than impact because this is a realization, not a blow. No text overlay — let the three words hit clean.

segments.text: In 2010, a twenty-four-year-old bank teller named Yesenia Guitron did something dangerous. She told the truth. She'd watched her colleagues at Wells Fargo open accounts that customers never asked for — credit cards ordered to addresses that didn't exist, savings accounts funded by moving money between other accounts without permission. She knew why they did it. There was a quota: every customer should have eight products. "Eight is Great." Miss the number and you get a warning. Miss it again and you get fired. So the tellers cheated. Because the alternative was unemployment.

beats.text: In 2010, a twenty-four-year-old bank teller named Yesenia Guitron did something dangerous.
She told the truth.
She'd watched coworkers open fake accounts in customers' names without their knowledge.

segments.notes: Cold open. Three beats mirror the three facts: who she is → what she did → what she saw. Generic whistleblower intro earns audience sympathy before Wells Fargo branding hits. Music full at top, drops to ducking as VO begins. Whoosh on 'dangerous' primes tension.

segments.text: Yesenia called the company's ethics hotline and reported the fraud. Wells Fargo terminated her the same week. She never found steady work in banking again. Her name went on an industry blacklist — a record that follows you like a scar.

beats.text: Yesenia called the company's ethics hotline and reported the fraud.
Wells Fargo terminated her the same week.
She never found another banking job. Wells Fargo had blacklisted her.

segments.notes: Three beats track the three acts of her punishment: reported → fired → blacklisted. Pause BEFORE segment entry lets the prior beat breathe. Impact SFX on 'terminated' is earned — this is a genuine reveal. Each Wells Fargo image is distinct to avoid visual repetition.

segments.text: Three point five million fake accounts. Five thousand three hundred tellers fired for opening them. And the woman who designed the quota — Carrie Tolstedt, head of Community Banking — kept fifty-seven million dollars and got zero prison time. She served her sentence at home. Ford's formula required a memo. Wells Fargo's didn't even require a decision — just a number and a threat.

beats.text: Three point five million fake accounts.
Five thousand three hundred tellers fired for opening them.
And the woman who denounced it — fired too.

segments.notes: No SFX — the statistics are the punch. One stat per beat creates rhythmic emphasis. Video cut on the final irony ('the woman who denounced it') signals we're pivoting from data to meaning. Measured tone holds before the broader pattern is revealed.

segments.text: Ford needed a document to do this. Wells Fargo only needed a quota. The next company didn't need either. It just needed a head start.

beats.text: Ford needed a document to do this.
Wells Fargo only needed a quota.
The next company didn't need either.
It just needed a prescription pad.

segments.notes: Three-company comparison, one visual per company method: Ford recall doc → Wells Fargo banking exec → generic boardroom (anticipation beat) → Purdue opioid footage. 1.5s pause BEFORE segment for anticipation. Each company gets its matching entity visual. Dissolve out into chapter card signals major topic shift. Music rises briefly at transition.

segments.text: Purdue Pharma saw the lawsuits coming a decade early and withdrew ten point seven billion dollars from the company before anyone could calculate the fine. Richard Sackler promised a, quote, blizzard of prescriptions at OxyContin's launch. In Kermit, West Virginia — population four hundred — a single pharmacy received nine million opioid pills in two years. The pharmacist went to prison. The Sacklers moved their money. More than eight hundred thousand Americans died. The settlement: seven point four billion. The family's remaining fortune: thirteen billion. Nine thousand dollars per death. Ford valued a life at two hundred thousand in 1977. The Sacklers got it down to nine thousand.

beats.text: Purdue Pharma saw the lawsuits coming a decade early.
And withdrew ten point seven billion dollars from the company before the settlement hit.
The Sackler family donated their name to museums.
While six hundred thousand Americans died from opioids.

segments.notes: Four beats: foreknowledge → extraction → cultural laundering → death toll. The juxtaposition of Guggenheim/Sackler name against opioid deaths is the entire argument in two images. 2s pause AFTER lets that juxtaposition land in silence before the thesis arrives.

segments.text: The fine is cheaper than the profit. Every time. Without exception.

beats.text: The fine is cheaper than the profit.
Every time. Without exception.

segments.text_overlay: THE FINE IS CHEAPER THAN THE PROFIT
segments.notes: Two deliberate beats. Visual 1 shows the scales metaphor (fine vs. profit). Visual 2 shows the financial documentation — abstract claim made concrete. Pause BEFORE creates anticipation. Pause AFTER creates silence runway into the thesis line. Text overlay reinforces the sub-thesis.

segments.text: The law doesn't prevent corporate crime. It prices it.

beats.text: The law doesn't prevent corporate crime.
It prices it.

sfx.motivation: Glass shatter on 'It prices it' — the illusion of justice breaking. Reserve for this single line in the entire video

segments.notes: The thesis line. The edit IS the argument: DOJ building (institutional authority) on 'doesn't prevent' → gavel tight shot on 'prices it.' The split makes viewers feel the pivot. 2s pause BEFORE is the longest in the video — earn it. Glass shatter is the only moment across all 8 segments that gets this SFX. Text overlay repeats only the payoff clause.

segments.text: And the price keeps dropping. Since 2000, corporations have paid over one trillion dollars in fines and settlements in the United States alone. One hundred and twenty-seven companies have each paid more than a billion. And here's the number that should end every argument about whether the system works: companies caught repeatedly pay smaller fines as a percentage of their revenue over time. Not larger. Smaller. The more you violate, the better the deal gets.

beats.text: And the price keeps dropping.
Since 2000, corporations have paid over one trillion dollars in fines and settlements in the United States alone.
One hundred and twenty-seven companies have each paid more than one billion dollars in penalties. And they are all still operating.

segments.notes: Three closing beats: abstract 'dropping' → the trillion stat → Congress (the institution that sets the price). Music rises here — the video closes with scale, not outrage. 3s pause AFTER the final beat before fade to black. Chapter card 'THE RECKONING' titles this section. No SFX — the number $1 trillion earns its own silence.

segments.text: Each company added one feature to the original calculation. Ford added a memo. Wells Fargo added plausible deniability. Purdue added preemption. Facebook added scale. But every one of them had something in common — the damage, at least in theory, could be reversed. Ford could recall the car. Wells Fargo could close the accounts. Purdue could stop making the pills.

beats.text: Each company added one feature to the original calculation.
Ford added a memo.
Wells Fargo added plausible deniability.

sfx.motivation: beat marker — 'Wells Fargo added plausible deniability' lands as an indictment, not just a fact

segments.notes: Formula evolution — one company per beat, one cut per name. Formula image establishes abstraction, then we get specific fast. Ford recall notice is documentary-specific (not generic Ford). Wells Fargo exec face closes with the impact SFX on the beat marker. 1s pause lets the deniability line breathe.

segments.text: Then the formula met the internet. And the damage became permanent.

beats.text: Then the formula met the internet.
And the damage became permanent.

sfx.motivation: pause marker — 'damage became permanent' is the chapter-closing thesis line; rumble builds into the 3s silence before THE DATA card

segments.notes: Two-beat bridge into THE DATA chapter. Data center = 'met the internet.' Abstract theft visual = 'damage became permanent.' Rumble SFX fires under that line. Then 3s silence + fade to black before the chapter card — LearnByLeo 5-step chapter transition steps 1-2.

segments.text: [CHAPTER: THE DATA]

beats.text: [CHAPTER: THE DATA]

segments.notes: 3s silence from seg 1's pause marker, then fade from black with chapter card. Music raises during the card beat (step 3-4 of LearnByLeo chapter transition). Facebook-specific data center as first establishing visual of the chapter — not generic servers, these belong to the company we're about to indict. Music ducks again when narration resumes in seg 3.

segments.text: Facebook was the bridge between the old formula and the new one.

beats.text: Facebook was the bridge between the old formula and the new one.

segments.notes: Chapter hook — single clean establishing beat. Facebook HQ exterior, entity-matched. 'FACEBOOK' lower-third text overlay formally introduces the subject. Single shot because the sentence is a thesis statement that needs room. Visual variety accelerates immediately in seg 4.

segments.text: In 2013, a Cambridge University researcher named Aleksandr Kogan built a personality quiz app. Two hundred and seventy thousand people downloaded it. But Facebook's API — the system that connects apps to the platform — gave the quiz access to not just those users' data, but all of their friends' data too. Every like, every post, every photo, every connection. Two hundred and seventy thousand downloads became eighty-seven million people's data harvested in weeks.

beats.text: In 2013, a Cambridge University researcher named Aleksandr Kogan built a personality quiz app.
Two hundred and seventy thousand people downloaded it.
And through Facebook's API, it harvested the data of two hundred and seventy million users.

segments.notes: Three-beat escalation tracking the 1000x multiplier: researcher (Cambridge Analytica footage, documentary feel) → bar chart dramatizes the download count as a spike → Facebook data centers showing the mass harvest at scale. Text overlay '270,000 → 270,000,000' sits on beats 2-3 and IS the visual argument. The math is the horror. 1.5s pause after '270 million' lands before next beat marker.

segments.text: Facebook knew this was possible. It was a feature, not a bug — they'd designed the API to be open because open APIs drive engagement, and engagement drives advertising revenue. In 2014, they quietly changed the rules. But they never enforced deletion of the data already taken.

beats.text: Facebook knew this was possible.
It was a feature, not a bug — they'd designed the API to be open because open APIs drive developer adoption and developer adoption drives growth.

segments.notes: Beat marker = 1s pause BEFORE 'Facebook knew this was possible' — this is an accusation, not just a fact. The pause before lets the viewer feel the weight of complicity. HQ exterior on beat 1 (they're watching us) → data center on beat 2 (the mechanism). 'FEATURE, NOT A BUG' text overlay on beat 2 is the quotable thesis line for this section — ColdFusion-style graphic that stays on screen through the API explanation. Different Facebook HQ source (wiki) from seg 3 (pexels) to avoid visual repetition.

segments.text: Cambridge Analytica used that data to build voter profiles so precise they could predict what would make you angry before you felt it. They were hired by the Trump campaign. They were hired by groups supporting Brexit.

beats.text: Cambridge Analytica used that data to build voter profiles so precise
they could predict what would make you angry before you knew yourself.

segments.notes: Cambridge Analytica footage second use at a different start point (20s in) so it reads as new footage. Cut to European Parliament voting chamber — voters are the ultimate target, and this makes the abstract personal. Impact SFX fires on the anger-prediction beat marker. 1.5s pause after 'before you knew yourself' — the viewer needs a beat to sit with that.

segments.text: Eighty-seven million people's personalities — measured, modeled, and weaponized — for the price of a free quiz they never took. And most of them still don't know. A 2019 Pew survey found that seventy-four percent of Facebook users didn't know the platform maintained a list of their interests and traits for ad targeting. They didn't know they'd been profiled. They didn't know their data had been sold. They just knew that their feed felt different in 2016 — angrier, more anxious, more polarized — and they assumed that was the world changing. It wasn't the world. It was the algorithm. Tuned by their own data, sold without their consent, deployed to shape an election.

beats.text: Eighty-seven million people's personalities —
measured, modeled, and weaponized —
for the price of a free quiz they never knew they were taking.

sfx.motivation: beat + pause markers — the illusion of consent shatters on 'free quiz they never knew they were taking'; glass shatter = the most visceral SFX choice for destroyed trust

segments.notes: Three-beat chapter climax with a clear visual grammar: scale (data center, 87M people as a number) → mechanism (AI/modeling company, clinical and cold) → face of accountability (Zuckerberg in Senate, the only human in three beats). '87 MILLION PEOPLE' text overlay stays on beat 1. Glass shatter on the final beat marker — the consent illusion breaks. Two beat markers + pause marker = SFX on first beat marker, then glass shatter fires on second beat marker as narration hits 'quiz.' 3s pause closes the chapter. Fade to black ends the segment. Different Facebook data center source (wiki_1) from seg 5 beat 2 (wiki_0) to avoid direct visual repeat.

segments.text: When the story broke in March 2018, Zuckerberg was summoned before Congress. He wore a suit. He said sorry. And then something happened that tells you everything about why the formula survives.

beats.text: When the story broke in March 2018,
Zuckerberg was summoned before Congress.
He wore a suit.
He said sorry. And then something happened.

segments.notes: Cold open with four distinct cuts matching the sentence rhythm. Cambridge Analytica establishes why he was summoned. Capitol gives institutional weight. Zuckerberg face-on in the chair is the visual anchor. Final still holds — the pause before the pivot creates anticipation without VO manipulation.

segments.text: A United States senator — a person with the power to regulate the most valuable company on Earth — looked at Mark Zuckerberg and asked: "How does Facebook make money if the product is free?"

beats.text: A United States senator — a person with the power to regulate the most valuable company on Earth —
looked at Mark Zuckerberg
and asked him a question.

segments.notes: Three-beat power buildup. Security-ringed Capitol (imposing, institutional) → Zuckerberg tight face (composed, waiting) → wide two-shot (power dynamic visible). Half-second pause after 'a question' before seg 2 lands the quote. Entity match: Zuckerberg-specific images throughout.

segments.text: Zuckerberg paused. And said: "Senator, we run ads."

beats.text: Zuckerberg paused.
And said: "Senator, we run ads."

segments.notes: The [beat] marker earns a 1.5s VO pause. Still image holds the silence — his face carries the moment. Cut to hearing clip at 30s offset (different framing than seg 0). Text overlay burns in on the quote. No SFX here; the pause and text overlay are the punctuation. Comedy framing, not yet sinister.

segments.text: The room laughed. The internet turned it into a meme. For weeks, the clip circulated as comedy — an old senator, a young CEO, a punchline about boomers not understanding technology.

beats.text: The room laughed.
The internet turned it into a meme. For weeks, the clip circulated as comedy —
an old senator, a young tech billionaire, and the gap between them.

segments.notes: Energy dip — this is the comedy beat before the hard pivot. Wide hearing shot shows the collective reaction. Reddit is shorthand for the internet sharing cycle; the scrolling interface reads as viral spread. Final wide shot reframes the 'gap' as the actual thesis. Keep music light here.

segments.text: And it was funny. It genuinely was. The man in charge of regulating the most valuable company on Earth didn't know how it made money. That's objectively absurd. It's the kind of thing you'd write into a satire and worry it was too on the nose.

beats.text: And it was funny. It genuinely was.
The man in charge of regulating the most valuable company on Earth
didn't know how it worked.

segments.notes: Confirm the joke before weaponizing it. Zuckerberg face (we're still laughing with them) → Capitol exterior (the regulator, stately and ignorant) → Facebook HQ (the regulated, gleaming and knowing). The juxtaposition does the pivot work. Half-second pause sets up seg 5's cold open.

segments.text: But here's what nobody said at the time. That hearing was the formula protecting itself. The people who set the fines — who write the regulations, who are supposed to be the ceiling on corporate behavior — didn't understand the business model of the company they were interrogating. And Zuckerberg knew it. He sat there, patient and composed, and explained his own business to the people who were supposed to be punishing him. He wasn't being grilled. He was giving a tutorial. And everyone watched it happen and laughed — because it was easier to laugh than to realize what it meant.

beats.text: But here's what nobody said at the time.
That hearing was the formula protecting itself.
The people who set the fines — they were the ones who didn't understand.

segments.notes: This is the video's first thesis beat. Three [beat] markers mean three hammer blows. 1.5s VO pause before the segment to let seg 4's observation sit. Impact SFX fires at the top. Each beat escalates: personal observation → systemic framing → structural indictment. Text overlay appears on beat 2.

segments.text: The people who set the fines don't understand what they're fining. The companies being fined have always known that.

beats.text: The people who set the fines don't understand what they're fining.
The companies being fined have always known that.

segments.notes: [beat] before, [pause] after. Two beats, two institutions, one power imbalance. DOJ building — austere, bureaucratic, sincere, outmatched. Corporate boardroom — polished, deliberate, smiling. The 2s VO pause after 'always known that' is the gut-punch landing. Text overlay burns in on beat 2. Rumble SFX fires under the final line.

segments.text: The FTC investigated for over a year. In July 2019, they announced the largest fine in their history: five billion dollars.

beats.text: The FTC investigated for over a year.
In July 2019, they announced the largest fine in their history:
five billion dollars.

segments.notes: The fine as the proof point for everything above. Settlement document (institutional, credible, slow) → news broadcast (media treated it as accountability) → stat graphic (the number that will be interrogated in the next section). '$5 BILLION' text overlay on final beat sets up the implicit question the video will answer: was that a punishment, or a price?

segments.text: Here is what five billion dollars means to Facebook. Revenue that year: seventy point seven billion. The fine was seven percent. Net profit: eighteen point five billion. The fine was about twenty-seven percent of one year's profit — paid once, for a violation that ran for years and compromised eighty-seven million people.

beats.text: Here is what five billion dollars means to Facebook.
Revenue that year: seventy point seven billion.
The fine was seven percent of that.

segments.notes: Three tight beats matching each sentence: fine announcement footage → revenue scale (profit chart) → the ratio (Facebook fine image). Text overlay drives the key stat. The beat marker signals a breath before we go into the vote. No SFX — saving them for the earned reveals.

segments.text: The FTC vote was three to two. Party line. The two dissenting commissioners didn't think the fine was too harsh. They thought it was too lenient. They wanted to sue, not settle. They wanted to hold Zuckerberg personally liable. They lost.

beats.text: The FTC vote was three to two. Party line.
The two dissenting commissioners didn't think the fine was too harsh. They thought it wasn't enough.

segments.notes: Two beats: institutional (Capitol building = the regulatory body) → human faces of dissent (the people who wanted more). Text overlay '3–2 VOTE' makes the partisan split concrete. The micro-reveal — dissenters wanted MORE — lands on the face cut. Pause after for the irony to register.

segments.text: On July twelfth, when the fine amount leaked, Facebook's stock rose one percent. The market had expected worse. Investors were relieved. Mark Zuckerberg's net worth increased by one point one billion dollars that day. He made more from the announcement of the fine than the fine cost the company. The market's verdict was clear: this is the ceiling. This is the worst it gets. And the worst it gets is a good day.

beats.text: On July twelfth, when the fine amount leaked,
Facebook's stock rose one percent.
The market had expected worse. Investors had priced in ten billion.

sfx.motivation: hard impact on the stock-rose cut — the market rewarding law-breaking is the core outrage of this chapter, fully earned

segments.notes: The highest tension beat in the Facebook section. Three cuts: news leak → Facebook stock chart (impact SFX here) → traders celebrating. Impact SFX is earned — the market going UP on a fine is genuinely disturbing. Extended pause after (2.5s) to let the contradiction sit. Text overlay makes it undeniable.

segments.text: Now. After everything I've just shown you — Ford, Wells Fargo, Purdue, Facebook — you'd be forgiven for thinking the formula is unbeatable. That this is just how it works. Fine, settle, move on. Nobody learns. Nothing changes.

beats.text: Now. After everything I've just shown you — Ford, Wells Fargo, Purdue, Facebook —
you'd be forgiven for thinking the formula is permanent. Untouchable.

segments.notes: Deliberate decompression — reflective summary before the pivot. Corporate fines image covers the roll call of Ford/WF/Purdue/Facebook. Mathematical formula image visually sets up the idea we are about to challenge. No SFX, no overlay — the quiet is intentional. The audience needs to believe the formula is unbeatable before we break it.

segments.text: But something happened in 2023 that proves the formula can break.

beats.text: But something happened in 2023 that proves the formula can break.

segments.notes: The fulcrum of the documentary. 2-second pause BEFORE (maximum anticipation, required by LearnByLeo pause-before-reveals rule). Single beat, single clip — GDPR/Meta/Ireland footage is exact entity match. Chapter card 'THE EXCEPTION' reframes everything. Whoosh on the cut. Music rises out of ducking state. Text overlay '2023' anchors the timeline.

segments.text: Ireland fined Meta one point two billion euros under Europe's GDPR — a law that scales fines to four percent of global annual revenue. Not a negotiated number. Not a fixed ceiling. A percentage.

beats.text: Ireland fined Meta one point two billion euros under Europe's GDPR —
a law that scales fines to four percent of global annual revenue.

segments.notes: Two beats: the fine and its source (GDPR regulation imagery) → the mechanism that makes it different (European Parliament voting). The insight is '4% of global revenue' — that's what scared Facebook. European Parliament image specifically shows the legislative body that created the scaling mechanism. Text overlay makes the number undeniable.

segments.text: And Facebook — the same Facebook that turned a five-billion-dollar American fine into a stock rally — panicked.

beats.text: And Facebook — the same Facebook that turned a five-billion-dollar American fine into a stock rally —
panicked.

segments.notes: Deliberate callback structure — the stock trading image echoes Seg 2, making the contrast visceral. Cut to cold Facebook HQ on 'panicked.' No SFX — silence lands harder than any hit here. The single word 'panicked' is the beat marker. Extended pause after lets it breathe. The word does the work.

segments.text: Within weeks, they rewrote their entire data transfer infrastructure. They shut down a pipeline they'd run for a decade. They rebuilt their European architecture from scratch. They didn't fight it in court for years. They didn't issue a press release and wait for it to blow over. They fixed it. Immediately. Because for the first time, the violation was more expensive than the profit.

beats.text: Within weeks, they rewrote their entire data transfer infrastructure.
They shut down a pipeline they'd run for a decade.

segments.notes: Concrete proof of behavioral change — physical infrastructure being rewritten. Generic data center clip → Facebook-specific data center image (entity match on the second beat). Long 3s pause after for the conclusion to land. Dissolve out signals chapter close. This is the thesis proof: a fine scaled to revenue FORCED actual change. The formula can break. Text overlay confirms the action.

segments.text: Sit with that for a second. The formula — the one that has survived five decades, across every industry, through every administration — broke. In Europe. Because someone changed one variable: they made the fine proportional.

beats.text: Sit with that for a second.
The formula — the one that has survived five decades, across every industry,
through every attempt to stop it — is still running. Right now.

segments.notes: Pause before segment lets prior revelation land. Formula image for 'sit with that' — keeps the thesis visual in frame. Scales of profit for 'across every industry' shows the breadth. Cost-of-doing-business footage as the final beat: ominous, confirms the formula is operational right now, not historical.

segments.text: Same company. Same executives. Same data. The only difference was the math. And when the math changed, the behavior changed overnight.

beats.text: Same company. Same executives. Same data.
The only difference was the math.
And when the math changed, the behavior changed. That's the proof. The formula is real.

segments.notes: Two [beat] markers mean narrator punches each of the three opening lines as separate stabs — Wells Fargo image holds across all three since the entity stays constant. Hard cut to math formula image on the pivot sentence. Boardroom image for the conclusion: suits deciding the math, behavior following mechanically. Impact SFX fires on 'The formula is real.' Text overlay reinforces the declarative thesis for visual-only viewers.

segments.text: Here's a thought experiment. A tripwire designed to catch one thing: an AI company scraping Reddit's content without permission.

segments.text: When Ford got caught, they could recall the car. When Facebook got caught, they could — in theory — delete the data. When Purdue got caught, they could stop manufacturing the pills. The damage was reversible. Expensive, slow, and nobody ever did it voluntarily. But the off switch existed.

beats.text: When Ford got caught, they could recall the car.

When AI got caught...

segments.notes: Three-beat structural comparison — each entity gets its own specific visual. Ford Pinto explosion clip is 5s, perfect for the beat. Facebook DATA CENTER (not HQ) shows what gets 'deleted.' AI scraping clip cuts off on the unresolved '...' — deliberate cliff edge into Seg 2.

segments.text: With AI, there is no off switch. When a model trains on scraped data, that data dissolves into the model's parameters like sugar dissolved in water. You cannot un-dissolve it. You cannot identify which outputs came from which inputs. You cannot point to a sentence and say "that came from Reddit" or "that came from a children's book published in 2019." The data becomes the model. The violation becomes the product. Every response the AI generates, every image it creates, every answer it provides — built on content taken without permission and impossible to return.

beats.text: With AI, there is no off switch.

segments.notes: Beat + pause markers both here — 1.5s pause before is the anticipation window. Impact SFX fires at the top of the beat. Text overlay locks in the thesis line. segments.text: Even if every AI company loses every lawsuit, they keep the models. The models keep running. The products keep generating revenue. The fine doesn't undo the training. It just pays for the data after the fact — like shoplifting and mailing a check later. Except the check is always less than the retail price.

segments.text: And the people who try to stop it? Remember Yesenia Guitron — the Wells Fargo teller who called the ethics hotline and was fired for it? The formula punishes the people who resist it. It rewards the people who run it. That pattern repeats in every industry, in every decade.

She created promotional work for Hulu. Art was her full-time job for four years. She'd built something.

segments.text: Every illustration she'd spent months creating. Every piece that defined her style. Scraped, indexed, and fed into a model that anyone could now use to generate images that look like her work — for free. A publisher she'd worked with for two years emailed to say they were "exploring AI-generated options" for their next cover. Her commissions dropped. Her online sales fell. The style she'd spent a decade developing could now be approximated in seconds by typing a sentence into a box. She started pivoting to 3D art — not because she wanted to, but because she hoped three-dimensional work would be harder to scrape.

segments.text: Chris Vialpondo is a renter in Seattle's Lower Queen Anne neighborhood. In 2022, he opened a notice from his property manager and learned his rent had increased by fifty percent. Same apartment. Same neighborhood. Same job. He was already working two jobs to make rent. Fifty percent meant the difference between getting by and going under. It meant counting every grocery trip. It meant the constant math of which bill gets paid this week and which one waits. He reached out to his property manager — the human being he thought had set the price — and was told nothing could be done. Because his property manager hadn't set the price. A company he'd never heard of had.

segments.text: RealPage. A company that takes confidential pricing data from competing landlords — data that competitors are not legally supposed to share — and feeds it into an algorithm that recommends rent prices across more than thirteen million apartments. Ninety percent of landlords follow the recommendation. The result: coordinated rent increases across buildings that are supposed to be competing with each other. The Department of Justice found that the algorithm costs renters an average of seventy dollars a month more — and over a hundred dollars a month in six major metro areas.

segments.text: Europe figured this out. Four percent of global revenue. Proportional. Automatic. No ceiling. When the fine scales with the company, the formula breaks. Facebook shrugged off a five-billion-dollar American fine and panicked over a European one. The tools exist. Criminal liability for executives — not the tellers, the architects. Disgorgement — hand back every dollar earned from the violation, not a negotiated fraction. The legal frameworks are built. The question has never been how. The question is why.

He grew up carrying scars that covered his body and a verdict that was supposed to change things — one hundred and twenty-five million dollars, reduced to three point five million. The message was: we've done the math, and your pain has a price. Ford paid it and moved on.

They kept thirteen billion. And they kept the wall.

segments.text: The Grush-Saunby memo put a dollar value on a human life in 1977. Two hundred thousand dollars. Purdue's settlement valued each opioid death at nine thousand. Facebook's fine valued each compromised user at fifty-seven dollars. The AI settlements value each stolen book at three thousand dollars. Elliana's illustrations? Not priced yet. Your Reddit posts? Your YouTube comments? Your blog from 2016?
